elements.id-string-5: \vspace{-0.15in}We present Citadel, to our knowledge, the first side-channel-resistant enclave platform to run realistic secure programs on a speculative out-of-order multicore processor.First, we develop a new hardware mechanism to enable secure shared memory while defending against transient execution attacks.Then, we develop an efficient dynamic cache partitioning scheme, improving both enclaves' and unprotected processes' performance.We conduct an in-depth security analysis and a performance evaluation of our new mechanisms.Finally, we build the hardware and software infrastructure required to run our secure enclaves.Our multicore processor runs on an FPGA and boots untrusted Linux from which users can securely launch and interact with enclaves.We open-source our end-to-end hardware and software infrastructure, hoping to spark more research and bridge the gap between conceptual proposals and FPGA prototypes.
elements.id-string-7: Secure Enclaves or Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) are powerful trusted-hardware primitives that can be seen as processes with strengthened privacy and integrity properties.

elements.id-string-79: Speculative or transient execution is one of the key performance features of modern processors.
elements.id-string-80: Unfortunately, it can make reasoning about security boundaries more difficult.
elements.id-string-81: Some microarchitectural data structures that orchestrate speculation (e.g., branch predictors) can be trained to execute snippets of existing code speculatively, in ways that are incorrect or on data that should not be accessed during normal execution.

elements.id-string-83: These erroneous executions happen speculatively and these instructions will end up being squashed by the processor.
elements.id-string-84: Nonetheless, they will still leave traces in the microarchitectural state of the machine.
elements.id-string-85: For example, a speculative load to some data will not affect the values of the architectural registers but will load the data in the memory hierarchy and possibly change the state of caches.
elements.id-string-86: The changes in the microarchitectural state are not directly observable by the attacker but can be extracted using a microarchitectural timing side channel.
elements.id-string-87: This means that a program that manages sensitive data can be coerced into leaking private data speculatively through a microarchitectural side channel.

elements.id-string-116: Given the threat model, our high-level security goals for our platform are three-fold: privacy, integrity and availability.

elements.id-string-152: Our first attempt at a new communication primitive is called secure drawer.
elements.id-string-153: Very much like the ones used at bank counters, a secure drawer is a memory region that can be filled up by one security domain and then pushed and pulled by another security domain to access it.
elements.id-string-154: This primitive has clear security boundaries as no security domains have concurrent access to the same memory region.
elements.id-string-155: Nevertheless, it has important performance drawbacks as it can only manipulate coarse memory regions as defined by the underlying physical memory partitioning primitive (32MB in our case) and several SM calls are required to push and pull the memory region.

elements.id-string-157: Finally, the enclave programmer needs to modify their application to deal with the new primitive and potentially different address spaces, move all the require data around, and handle concurrency correctly.

elements.id-string-176: Sanctum \cite{costan2016sanctum} already presents hardware mechanisms for memory isolation in the context of an untrusted OS.
elements.id-string-177: Like RISC-V Physical Memory Protection (PMP) \cite{waterman2015risc}, Sanctum introduces a mechanism to partition physical memory and prevent a malicious OS to access another security domain's private memory regions.
elements.id-string-178: At its core, the mechanism uses two 64-bit registers per core (one for trusted memory and one for untrusted memory) as memory bitmaps.
elements.id-string-179: Each bit represents a same size physical memory region (typically 32MB) and functions as an access-rights flag for the currently-running program.
elements.id-string-180: Citadel borrows this mechanism for its simplicity.

elements.id-string-183: Two new registers \texttt{TMVBASE} and \texttt{TMVMASK} are used to define \texttt{TMVRANGE} which corresponds to the trusted memory virtual range (the enclave's private memory in general).
elements.id-string-184: The SM enforces as an invariant that the physical memory mapped by \texttt{TMVRANGE} is owned by the corresponding security domain.
elements.id-string-185: When a memory access to a virtual address is performed by a program, one of the two page tables needs to be picked to translate the virtual address.
elements.id-string-186: If the virtual address falls in \texttt{TMVRANGE}, it corresponds to an address within trusted memory and the translation is performed using the \emph{trusted page table}.
elements.id-string-187: The trusted memory page table root is stored in another new register called \texttt{TMPTBR} accessible to the page walker.
elements.id-string-188: Another important invariant is that the trusted enclave page table is stored within trusted enclave memory.
elements.id-string-189: This is at first enforced by the SM during setup and then by the enclave itself.
elements.id-string-190: If the virtual address falls outside of \texttt{TMVRANGE}, it corresponds to an address in untrusted memory and the translation is performed using the \emph{untrusted page table}.
elements.id-string-191: The untrusted page table is managed by the OS and stored in untrusted memory.
elements.id-string-192: The root of the OS page table is stored in the standard \texttt{SATP} register.

elements.id-string-990: Hardware isolation primitives such as secure enclaves aim to protect sensitive programs, but remain vulnerable to transient execution attacks.Complete microarchitectural isolation is not a satisfactory defense mechanism as it leaves out public shared memory, critical for usability and application performance.Conversely, hardware-software co-designs for secure speculation can counter these attacks but are not yet practical, since they make assumptions on the speculation modes, the exposed microarchitectural state, and the software, which are all hard to support for the entire software stack.This paper advocates for processors to incorporate microarchitectural isolation primitives \emph{and} mechanisms for controlled speculation, enabling different execution modes.These modes can restrict what is exposed to an attacker,effectively balancing performance and program-analysis complexity.We introduce two mechanisms to securely share memory between an enclave and an untrusted OS in an out-of-order processor.We show that our two modes are complementary, achieving speculative non-interference with a reasonable performance impact, while requiring minimal code annotation and simple program analysis doable by hand.Our prototype, Citadel, is a multicore processor running on an FPGA, booting untrusted Linux, and supporting comprehensive enclave capabilities, such as shared memory, and remote attestation.To our knowledge, Citadel is the first end-to-end enclave platform to run secure applications, such as cryptographic libraries or small private inference workloads, on a speculative out-of-order multicore processor while protecting against a significant class of side-channel attacks.

elements.id-string-1345: Transient execution side-channel attacks, such as Spectre, have been shown to break almost all isolation primitives.We introduce a new security property we call \emph{relaxed microarchitectural isolation} (RMI) that allows \emph{sensitive} programs that are \emph{not-constant-time} to \emph{share memory} with an attacker while restricting the information leakage to that of non-speculative execution.Although this type of speculative security property is typically challenging to enforce, we show that we can leverage the \emph{enclave} setup to achieve it.In particular, we use microarchitectural isolation to restrict attacker's observations in conjunction with straightforward hardware mechanisms to limit speculation.This new design point presents a compelling trade-off between security, usability, and performance, making it possible to efficiently enforce RMI for \emph{any} program.We demonstrate our approach by implementing and evaluating two simple defense mechanisms that satisfy RMI: (1) \emph{Safe mode}, which disables speculative accesses to shared memory, and (2) \emph{Burst mode}, a localized performance optimization that requires simple program analysis on small code snippets.Our end-to-end prototype, Citadel, consists of an FPGA-based multicore processor that boots Linux and runs secure applications, including cryptographic libraries and private inference, with less than 5\% performance overhead.

elements.id-string-1588: Safe mode: Preventing Speculative Shared Memory
elements.id-string-1589: Our first approach consists of preventing speculative shared memory accesses altogether, effectively removing any speculative transmitters that can reach the attacker.
elements.id-string-1590: This approach enforces RMI for any program without extra program analysis, making it a great foundational mode to use by default.
elements.id-string-1591: We illustrate this principle by building a simple mechanism.
elements.id-string-1592: \emph{Safe} mode identifies unsafe shared memory accesses early in the memory execution pipeline, delaying their translation and processing until they become non-speculative (i.e., reach the head of the reorder buffer (ROB)).
elements.id-string-1593: This is similar \emph{in spirit} to delay-on-miss~\cite{sakalis2019efficient} but only delays \emph{shared} memory accesses and cannot leverage the L1 cache for reasons expressed in section \ref{sec:disentangle}.

elements.id-string-1596: Safe instructions proceed to the next \MemExePipeline{} stage; unsafe ones are squashed and signaled to the reservation station so they are re-dispatched once they become non-speculative.

elements.id-string-1600: Our second approach, called \emph{Burst} mode, is a hardware-software co-design that can improve performance for specific code snippets.
elements.id-string-1601: It allows some speculative accesses to shared memory (i.e. $\uarch[burst]{\cdot}{} \vdash \contract[shm]{\cdot}{stl}$) but ensures that it only runs programs that will not leak secrets (i.e. only runs $p$ if $p \vdash NI(\contract[shm]{\cdot}{seq} \Rightarrow \contract[shm]{\cdot}{stl})$).

elements.id-string-1603: In order to simplify this analysis, we apply two simple design principles: 1) we ensure the (speculative) control flow of our code snippet is self-contained 2) we constrain speculation to a simple model where it is not attacker-controlled.
elements.id-string-1604: The first principle indicates that we should deactivate any predictors that enable speculative jumps to arbitrary locations and guard our code snippets with speculative barriers.
elements.id-string-1605: The second stems from the fact that disabling more predictors helps simplify program analysis.
elements.id-string-1606: Following these principles, we implement a simple static branch predictor, which enables shared memory pipelining on Citadel (disabled in \emph{Safe mode}).
elements.id-string-1607: According to our first guidelines, we disable the branch target buffer (BTB), and the return address stack (RAS) (Figure \ref{fig:fetchpipe}).
elements.id-string-1608: This is done on demand by writing to a new CSR, using a write instruction that also doubles as a speculation barrier.
elements.id-string-1609: Following our second principle, we also disable the branch history table (BHT), effectively implementing straight-line speculation \cite{straightlinespecARM, guarnieri2021hardware} where the only prediction is the hardcoded ``\texttt{pc+4}'', predicting the next instruction without a change in control flow.
